method.reason: Attempts can be counted: the IDS logged 14 exploit-signature alerts from allowlisted ranges and there is an April 2026 incident of key guessing. No loss history exists for these servers, so a direct LEF estimate is not supported. Evidence on attacker capability and control strength is not on a 0 to 100 scale, so vulnerability is estimated directly.

estimates.rationale: The IDS raised 14 exploit-signature alerts from allowlisted ranges in 12 months (evidence 5), each a probable exploit attempt. Incident INC-2026-021 shows a compromised customer network was used against the servers (evidence 7). 2,150 failed key authentications are mostly misconfiguration, a weak signal (evidence 4). Nine broad allowlist ranges widen exposure (evidence 11), and nine phished corporate accounts give a small internal-foothold contribution (evidence 13). The 1.84M blocked connections are background scanning that never reached the service, so they are not counted (evidence 3). The most likely value sits slightly above the 14 observed alerts to allow for undetected attempts and the post-support period; the range is wide.

The OS has had no patches since January 2026, with six published vulnerabilities, two critical and one with a public exploit (evidence 9). The SFTP service is three releases behind and cannot be fixed on this OS (evidence 10). Against this, none of the 14 exploit alerts succeeded and there were no confirmed compromises in 36 months (evidence 6). That is weak evidence, since the OS only lost support in January 2026. The pen test (evidence 12) was run from a non-allowlisted address and not repeated after end of support, so it adds little. Key-only authentication does not stop pre-authentication exploits. The CVE details are still open (data request 1), so the range is wide and confidence low.

INC-2026-021 cost 45 response hours at the $150 loaded rate, or $6,750, for an attempt with no access (evidence 7, 8). A real compromise of servers holding payroll data would need much more work: forensics, rebuilding the servers, and customer coordination. The most likely value is roughly 100 hours at $150, with a high end of about 600 hours. These multiples are judgement, not measured, so confidence is low.

method.reason: Telemetry lets us count attempts (failed logins, lockouts, spraying bursts, phished accounts), so threat event frequency times vulnerability fits. There is no confirmed loss history, and the zero confirmed events in 36 months is weak evidence given low detection coverage. A pen test gives a direct success rate for vulnerability.

estimates.rationale: Security Telemetry shows 3 suspected password-spraying bursts in 12 months (id 17), but the review was one-off so coverage is limited. There were 310 lockouts (id 16) and 9,400 failed logins (id 15), which show frequent guessing. 9 corporate accounts were phished in 12 months, 2 of them support engineers (id 19), so foothold events happen several times a year. MITRE valid-account abuse (id 23) supports the paths. I take a threat event as a deliberate attempt against the console. The range allows for undercounting because nothing alerts on the logs.

The internal pen test (PT-058, id 21) got valid credentials by spraying in 2 of 3 attempts and then reached tenant data, which points to high vulnerability once an attacker is inside the network. Real attackers are likely less skilled and less persistent than testers, and the 310 lockouts (id 16) show lockout does stop some guessing. The finding (FND-0988, id 20) shows 140 of 220 users already on MFA, so about 64% of accounts are protected and exposure is shrinking. The 80 users still without MFA remain open. Which of the 35 impersonation accounts are among them is an open question (data request 13). MITRE password spraying (id 22) confirms the technique avoids per-account lockout. The range is wide because the sample is only 3 tests.

The Asset Inventory (id 14) shows the console reaches all Nova customer tenant data. About 9.5M individuals have records and about 3,100 customers depend on it. It is Restricted and Tier 1. A confirmed breach of this data would very likely lead to customer and regulator reactions. No internal history of such an event exists, so the range is wide and confidence is low.

estimates.rationale: Security Telemetry Row 10 (id 30) shows 9 corporate accounts confirmed compromised by phishing in 12 months, 2 of them support engineers. Engineers who can edit pipelines are a subset of the workforce, so the rate of engineer-account compromises that could reach the pipeline is below 9 a year. I used a most likely value of about 3 and a high of 9, the corporate total. Row 11 (id 31) shows 1,260 pipeline changes a year, so a hostile edit has many chances to blend in. Row 12 (id 32) shows 2 alerts from outside the pipeline range, both benign. That is not proof of zero attacks. Key-leak and dependency attempts are not counted (request 19 is open), so confidence is low.

The May 2026 penetration test (id 29) showed a tester with a standard engineer account edited a pipeline definition and gained production admin. The single reviewer approved it without noticing, so the skill needed is low. The wildcard policy (FND-1220, id 27) means any foothold gives full access. The 14-month-old long-lived keys (FND-1221, id 28) add a second path. The SIEM alerts (id 32) work but do not block access. One pen test is a small sample and real attackers must first get a foothold, so the range is wide. The most likely value is 70%.

The production account is classified Restricted and holds time and attendance data for about 3.4 million individuals, with about 2,300 dependent customers (Asset Inventory Asset-355, id 25). A confidentiality breach of that size would very likely require regulator notification and draw customer reactions. Whether every event reaches that scale depends on how much data the attacker actually reads, so the range is wide. Legal's request 18 on notification duties is still open, so confidence is low.

The 2024 incident (INC-2024-077) took 60 response hours at the 150 USD/hour loaded labor rate, which is 9,000 USD with no other direct costs. That is used as the most likely value. The low end assumes a quicker case with fewer records viewed (about 20 hours). The high end allows a broader investigation of many stale accounts (about 200 hours). Confidence is medium because this is one internal event on the same asset.

method.reason: Attempts can be counted: the web proxy logged 420 uploads to personal cloud storage in 30 days, and there is one confirmed loss event (INC-2025-090). One event in history is too thin to estimate LEF directly, so TEF times vulnerability fits better, with the incident as a cross-check.

estimates.rationale: Security Telemetry Row 15 shows 420 uploads to personal cloud storage in 30 days from 37 users, but upload content is not visible, so most are likely benign. Open request 46 asks how many looked like extracts. Incident INC-2025-090 shows one deliberate-style attempt (an emailed extract) in the history. Malware and phished-account context (EDR 11 detections, 9 compromised accounts) adds a little. The range counts only attempts to move extracts out, not all uploads. It is wide and low confidence because the share of uploads that were extracts is unknown, and USB use is not counted (request 45 is open).

No DLP, egress monitoring or USB and cloud blocking exists on these workstations, so most attempts to copy extracts would succeed. The October 2025 audit (CT-275) failed, with 9 of 20 workstations holding old extracts, which also shows weak data handling. The one confirmed event (INC-2025-090) was recovered, so controls such as ticket approval or detection after the fact sometimes help. The range is wide because the audit does not show how many attempts actually got through, and EDR is not built to catch user copying. Evidence on the cloud and USB paths is from MITRE ATT&CK only.

Incident INC-2025-090 cost 47,000 USD: 180 response hours at the 150 USD/hour loaded labor rate (27,000 USD) plus 20,000 USD of other direct costs. That is the most likely value. The low end assumes a faster, smaller response. The high end allows for a larger or less contained event, since the asset holds extracts of varying size and the Restricted class implies heavier investigation. Confidence is medium because it rests on one internal incident.

In the single confirmed event, INC-2025-090, one customer was notified, so that event did draw an outside reaction. One event is not a rate. A recovered personal-email copy drew a reaction, so a copy that leaves the company without recovery is more likely to draw one. The range is wide and low confidence. Legal (request 48) and record counts (request 47) are still open.

Incident INC-2025-090 affected 5,100 records and led to notification of one customer. That gives a scale for notification, call handling and customer follow-up. The 47,000 USD primary cost already includes the incident's other direct costs, so this range covers only the extra work in a larger exposure. The high end allows for a bigger extract or several customers, since typical extract size is unknown (request 47 open). The figures are judgement scaled from one incident, so confidence is low.

method.reason: There is loss history for this exact asset (the June 2025 failed-change incident), so loss event frequency can be estimated directly. estimates.rationale: Incident History INC-2025-046 shows one loss event on Asset-208 since June 2025, a failed schema change that needed a restore. One event is weak evidence of frequency, and zero events in other periods would not mean zero frequency. The range is wide and centered on roughly one event every 2 to 3 years, with a ceiling of one per year. The org-wide phishing telemetry (id 63) applies only to ransomware and is not used for the numbers. Data request 53 on events across production databases is open and could narrow this.

Incident INC-2025-046 recorded 380 response hours, about $57,000 at the $150 per hour loaded labor rate (evidence 60). That anchors the most likely value. The 2025 restore took 5.5 hours. The last restore test (CT-340) suggests a restore now of roughly 9.5 hours if scaled linearly, so a slower restore, a failed restore or a ransomware event could need many more response hours. This is why the maximum is about 2.5 times the observed cost.

In the one observed event (INC-2025-046) SLA credits were paid even though the restore beat the 8-hour objective, which shows that customer-facing consequences followed. The asset inventory (Asset-208) says about 2,300 customers depend on this Tier 1 database and that SLA credits and notifications follow an availability outage. One event is a thin basis, so the range stays wide but high.

The incident record (INC-2025-046) shows $142,000 in other direct costs, which include SLA credits, after the failed change. This is the best available anchor for secondary response cost. The breakdown is not yet known (Finance request 56 is open), and the 2,300 dependent customers (asset inventory) mean a longer outage than 5.5 hours could cost more. The minimum allows for a smaller credit payout.

method.reason: There is one prior loss event, but the scenario covers a different path (account takeover and harvesting) and a much larger asset. Attempt-type telemetry exists (account compromises, clone alerts), so threat event frequency times vulnerability fits best. Vulnerability is estimated directly because there is no 0 to 100 capability and strength data.

estimates.rationale: Security Telemetry Row 10 shows 9 corporate accounts compromised by phishing in 12 months, but this is a base rate for all staff, not repository users. Only a share would have repository access (about 2,050 of the workforce), and not every takeover leads to cloning. Row 16 shows 4 large-clone alerts in 12 months, 3 benign and 1 unresolved contractor alert, which is weak evidence of harvesting. Incident INC-2025-012 shows a leaked key was used once since Feb 2025. The range runs from under one to the full 9 takeovers per year, with a most likely value of about 3. It stays wide and low confidence because the contractor alert is unresolved (request 60).

Once an attacker holds a repository account, the source code platform (Asset-846) holds embedded secrets, so harvesting is direct. Findings FND-1302 shows 185 of 212 secrets still unrotated after 27 were rotated. The Internal Audit review CT-298 failed, with only 38% of services using the vault, so resistance is weak. SSO and MFA reduce the chance an account is taken over, but that is counted in the takeover frequency. The remaining uncertainty is whether the attacker notices and successfully uses the secrets, and whether the database network limits stop use of the database credentials. The range is wide because the counts of production credentials and API keys are not yet known (request 61).

Incident INC-2025-012 cost 61,000 USD in total: 200 response hours at the 150 USD/hour loaded labor rate (30,000 USD) plus 31,000 USD other direct costs. That event involved one API key and no records. A takeover that reaches production databases would likely need many more hours, such as forensics and rotation of many secrets. The most likely value is the observed 61,000 USD, with a high end of about 250,000 USD (roughly 1,000 hours plus other costs). The low end assumes a quick, contained event. Confidence is low because there is only one past event and it was smaller.
